title: Antimatter: The Rare Twin of Matter That Vanishes on Contact
summary: Imagine a mirror world where every particle has a twin with the opposite electric charge. That's antimatter. For every electron, there's a positron. For every proton, an antiproton. They have the same mass but opposite charges — with one exception: the neutron and antineutron are both neutral. When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate. They destroy each other and release energy as gamma rays, a high-energy form of light. This makes antimatter incredibly difficult to store. If it touches ordinary matter, it's gone in a flash. So scientists use magnetic and electric fields to levitate antiparticles without touching anything. In March 2026, researchers at CERN transported antiprotons in a truck for the first time, using electromagnetic fields to keep them suspended. Antimatter is extremely rare in the universe. A tiny amount forms naturally when cosmic rays smash into Earth's atmosphere, and some radioactive decay produces antiparticles. But it never lasts long. Scientists believe the Big Bang created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. Yet today, ordinary matter dominates. Why? That's one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in physics. Researchers are searching for answers by studying antimatter and dark matter, hoping to unlock secrets from the universe's very first moments. Understanding antimatter could even explain why we exist at all. The mystery is personal: every particle of you has a mirror twin that vanished. Where did all the antimatter go? That question drives scientists at CERN and beyond. They trap antiparticles in magnetic and electric fields, study how they behave, and compare them with ordinary matter. Any tiny difference could hint at why matter survived and antimatter didn't. The answer may lie in the universe's very first moments, when matter and antimatter were created in equal amounts. By studying antimatter and dark matter, researchers hope to unlock those secrets — and explain why we exist at all.
why_it_matters: Antimatter research is a reminder that the most basic questions — why matter exists at all — still have no answer, and the tools being built now, such as better traps and the ability to transport antiparticles, are the groundwork for the next generation of physics.

background_read: CERN is the European Organization for Nuclear Research, a giant laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland, where many countries pool money and equipment to study particles; it runs the Large Hadron Collider, the biggest particle accelerator in the world. Antimatter was predicted mathematically by the British physicist Paul Dirac in 1928, and the positron was first spotted in 1932 when the American physicist Carl Anderson found its tracks in cosmic-ray data.

Antimatter is not only a laboratory curiosity: hospitals use positrons in PET scanners, where the gamma rays released as positrons annihilate with electrons inside a patient are used to build images of the body. Cosmic rays — fast particles from space — constantly strike Earth's atmosphere and create small amounts of antiparticles, but they vanish almost immediately on contact with ordinary matter.

The Big Bang is the leading explanation for how the universe began, expanding from an extremely hot, dense state. Because the rules of physics seem to treat matter and antimatter almost identically, the fact that ordinary matter dominates today is known as the matter–antimatter asymmetry, one of the deepest unsolved problems in physics. Precise comparisons between particles and their antimatter twins are how researchers hunt for the tiny difference that might explain it.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — fundamental science with real spin-offs
perspectives.description: Studying antimatter tests the deepest rules of physics and has already produced practical tools, since PET scanners in hospitals rely on positrons annihilating inside the body. The new ability to transport antiprotons by truck could let more labs run experiments that were previously possible only at CERN.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — vanishingly rare and enormously expensive
perspectives.description: Making antiparticles costs far more energy than the energy released when they annihilate, so antimatter will never be a practical fuel or power source. Critics argue that huge machines like those at CERN consume vast public funding for results that may take decades to matter.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a puzzle physicists have chased for generations
perspectives.description: Ever since Dirac predicted antimatter and Anderson found the positron, every precise test has shown antimatter behaving as a near-perfect mirror of matter, with only tiny asymmetries detected. That is exactly what makes the matter–antimatter asymmetry so stubborn: the expected difference keeps failing to show up at the scale needed to explain the universe.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — better traps, more precise tests
perspectives.description: Improved magnetic and electric trapping, plus portable transport such as the truck journey in March 2026, could allow comparisons of matter and antimatter at far higher precision than before. If a real difference is found, it might finally explain why anything survived the universe's first moments — and why we exist.
